lessonTitle: Central Venous Access and Knee Aspiration Anatomy

blocks.text: A patient in intensive care needs a central line and a drug that would damage a small peripheral vein. The operator finds the point where the two heads of a neck muscle meet the clavicle, feels the carotid pulse just medial, and enters the vein lying beside it. Every landmark in that sequence is anatomy, and each one protects a neighbouring structure.

blocks.markdown: A **central venous catheter** places its tip in a large central vein, usually the superior vena cava near the right atrium, so drugs are diluted quickly and pressures can be measured. Common entry veins are the internal jugular, subclavian and femoral veins. Modern practice uses real-time ultrasound to see the vein and surrounding structures; the surface landmarks below explain the anatomy that the ultrasound image displays and serve as a back-up.

blocks.title: Carotid sheath and the internal jugular vein
blocks.text: The internal jugular vein (IJV) runs in the carotid sheath with the common carotid artery medially and the vagus nerve posteriorly between them. It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid (SCM), emerging between the sternal and clavicular heads of that muscle in the lower neck, and joins the subclavian vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein.

blocks.markdown: **Landmarks for IJV cannulation.** Identify the triangle formed by the sternal head of SCM, the clavicular head of SCM and the upper border of the clavicle. The IJV lies at or just beneath its apex. The common carotid artery lies medial and slightly deeper, so you palpate it and keep your needle lateral to it. The right IJV is usually preferred because it runs almost straight to the right brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava, and the cupola of the pleura is lower on that side. Insertion in the lower neck risks the apex of the lung, so injury can cause a pneumothorax; carotid puncture and, on the left, damage to the thoracic duct are other risks.

blocks.title: Walking through an IJV approach
blocks.prompt: A surgeon asks you to identify the structures encountered from skin to vein using the apex of the SCM triangle.

steps.text: Palpate the sternal and clavicular heads of SCM and the clavicle to find the triangle.
Feel the carotid pulse medially and keep the needle path lateral to it.
The needle passes through skin, superficial fascia, platysma, then enters the gap between the two heads of SCM.
Deep to the muscle the IJV lies within the carotid sheath, lateral to the common carotid artery.
Withdrawal of dark, non-pulsatile blood confirms venous entry; bright pulsatile blood suggests the carotid artery.

blocks.answer: Skin, platysma, between the SCM heads, then the IJV in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery.

blocks.markdown: **Subclavian vein access.** The subclavian vein is the continuation of the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib. It arches over the first rib **anterior to scalenus anterior**, while the subclavian artery and the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus lie **posterior** to that muscle. The phrenic nerve descends on the front of scalenus anterior, and the cupola of the pleura and lung apex lie immediately behind and below the vein. In the infraclavicular approach the needle enters just below the clavicle, commonly taught at the junction of its medial and middle thirds, and is directed toward the suprasternal notch.

Just below clavicle, medial-middle third junction
Subclavian artery is posterior to scalenus anterior
Subclavian artery, pleura and lung apex, brachial plexus, phrenic nerve, thoracic duct (left)
Difficult, as the clavicle and rib lie nearby

blocks.title: Structures at risk in subclavian access
blocks.prompt: Predict which injury follows when a subclavian needle is advanced too deeply and posteriorly.

steps.text: Behind and below the vein lie the pleural cupola and lung apex.
A needle that goes too deep passes through the vein and pleura, allowing air into the pleural space.
The lung may collapse, causing a pneumothorax, with sudden dyspnoea and reduced breath sounds.
Posterior structures also include the subclavian artery and brachial plexus, so arterial puncture or arm paraesthesia may also follow.

blocks.answer: Pneumothorax is the main risk; arterial puncture and brachial plexus injury also follow.

blocks.markdown: **Knee joint aspiration.** The knee joint cavity extends above the patella as the **suprapatellar pouch** (bursa), which lies deep to the quadriceps tendon and communicates freely with the joint. Fluid collects there when there is an effusion. A commonly taught approach is to extend the knee, locate the superior pole of the patella, and insert the needle just lateral (or medial) to it, passing under the patella into the suprapatellar pouch. The structures nearby are the patella, quadriceps tendon, patellar retinacula, articular cartilage of the femoral condyles and, deeper, the capsule and synovial lining.

items: Position the knee extended with the quadriceps relaxed.
Palpate the patella and identify its superior pole.
Enter 1 cm lateral to the patella at that level, angling toward the suprapatellar pouch.
Avoid the articular cartilage and use strict aseptic technique to prevent introducing infection.

blocks.title: Always check the pulse before puncture
blocks.text: If blood is bright red and pulsatile in a neck line, the carotid has been entered. Do not dilate or insert the catheter; withdraw and apply pressure.

blocks.title: Use ultrasound where possible
blocks.text: Real-time ultrasound shows the vein, artery, pleura and needle tip, and reduces complications compared with landmark-only techniques, but surface anatomy remains the foundation.

points: The IJV lies lateral to the common carotid artery within the carotid sheath and emerges between the two heads of SCM; carotid puncture and pneumothorax are key risks.
The subclavian vein lies anterior to scalenus anterior; the artery and brachial plexus lie behind it and the pleura lies below and behind the vein.
Knee aspiration enters the suprapatellar pouch just beside the superior pole of the patella, near the patella, quadriceps tendon and femoral condyles.

questions.stem: Which landmark identifies the usual site for internal jugular vein puncture in the lower neck?

options.text: The apex of the triangle formed by the two heads of sternocleidomastoid and the clavicle
The midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid

questions.correctOptionText: The apex of the triangle formed by the two heads of sternocleidomastoid and the clavicle

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the vein lies at the apex of the triangle between the SCM heads and clavicle.
distractorRationale.b: The posterior border of SCM is used for the external jugular vein and plexus structures, not the IJV.
distractorRationale.c: The cricoid cartilage marks a level of the neck but not the puncture site.
distractorRationale.d: The angle of the mandible is a high landmark far from the lower neck site.

questions.explanation: The IJV emerges between the sternal and clavicular heads of SCM above the clavicle. The apex of this triangle is the usual entry point.

questions.stem: During IJV cannulation, a needle is accidentally advanced medially. Which structure is most at risk?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the carotid lies medial to the IJV within the carotid sheath.
distractorRationale.b: The subclavian vein lies lower and lateral.
distractorRationale.c: The phrenic nerve lies deep on scalenus anterior, lateral and posterior.
distractorRationale.d: The vertebral artery lies deeper, posterior to the carotid sheath.

questions.explanation: The common carotid artery runs medial to the IJV in the carotid sheath. Palpating the carotid pulse and keeping the needle lateral reduces the risk of puncture.

questions.stem: Why is the right IJV often preferred over the left for central line placement?

options.text: It has a straighter course to the SVC and the pleural dome is lower on the right
It is the only jugular vein that lies lateral to the carotid artery
It drains directly into the right atrium
It lies medial to the carotid artery

questions.correctOptionText: It has a straighter course to the SVC and the pleural dome is lower on the right

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the right IJV runs almost straight into the right brachiocephalic vein and SVC.
distractorRationale.b: Both internal jugular veins lie lateral to their carotid arteries, so this is not the reason.
distractorRationale.c: It joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein; it does not drain directly into the atrium.
distractorRationale.d: The IJV lies lateral to the carotid artery, not medial.

questions.explanation: The right IJV forms a nearly straight path to the SVC and the right pleural cupola is lower. The thoracic duct enters the left venous angle, so left-sided puncture risks chyle leak.

questions.stem: In the infraclavicular approach to the subclavian vein, which structure lies immediately behind and below the vein and is at risk of injury by a deep needle?

options.text: Cupola of the pleura and lung apex

questions.correctOptionText: Cupola of the pleura and lung apex

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the pleura and lung apex lie behind and below the subclavian vein.
distractorRationale.b: The great saphenous vein is in the leg.
distractorRationale.c: Hepatic veins are in the abdomen.
distractorRationale.d: The trachea is medial and further from the usual needle path.

questions.explanation: The pleural cupola lies directly posterior to the subclavian vein, so a needle advanced too far can cause a pneumothorax. This is why the needle is angled shallowly along the posterior surface of the clavicle.

questions.stem: Which muscle separates the subclavian vein anteriorly from the subclavian artery and brachial plexus posteriorly?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the vein is in front of scalenus anterior, the artery and plexus behind it.
distractorRationale.b: SCM is superficial to the IJV, not a divider between the vein and artery.
distractorRationale.c: Trapezius lies posteriorly and does not separate them.
distractorRationale.d: Pectoralis major lies in front of the chest and is not part of this relation.

questions.explanation: Scalenus anterior passes between the subclavian vein in front and the artery and brachial plexus behind. This arrangement explains why the artery and plexus are less likely to be hit by a needle aimed at the vein.

questions.stem: Aspiration of a knee effusion is performed by entering the suprapatellar pouch beside the patella.
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar pouch communicates with the joint and lies deep to the quadriceps tendon, so fluid collects in it. A needle entering beside the superior pole of the patella reaches it without crossing articular cartilage.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a swollen knee. When aspirating, the operator enters 1 cm lateral to the upper pole of the patella. Which structure lies deep to the quadriceps tendon at this site and holds the fluid?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the suprapatellar pouch lies above and behind the patella under the quadriceps tendon.
distractorRationale.b: The fat pad lies below the patella.
distractorRationale.c: The popliteal fossa is posterior to the knee.
distractorRationale.d: The medial meniscus lies within the joint on the medial tibial plateau.

questions.explanation: Fluid in a knee effusion collects in the suprapatellar pouch, which lies deep to quadriceps femoris. The entry point beside the upper pole of the patella leads into this pouch.

questions.stem: A needle is inserted into the IJV and blood returned is bright red and pulsatile. Explain the likely anatomical error and the structures that lie close to the IJV that were at risk.
markingGuide: Bright red and pulsatile blood suggests arterial entry.
The common carotid artery lies medial to the IJV in the carotid sheath.
Needle was directed too medially or too deeply.
Other nearby structures: vagus nerve, pleural dome, thoracic duct (left).
Management is to withdraw the needle and apply pressure rather than continue.
questions.explanation: The carotid artery runs alongside the IJV within the same sheath, so a misdirected needle can enter it. Recognition by colour and pulsatility prevents catheter placement into the artery.

questions.stem: List the structures at risk during subclavian vein access and give the anatomical relation of each.
markingGuide: Pleural cupola and lung apex behind and below the vein, risk of pneumothorax.
Phrenic nerve on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior.
questions.explanation: The subclavian vein crosses the first rib in front of scalenus anterior while the artery and plexus pass behind it. The pleura lies directly below and behind, which is why pneumothorax is the main complication.

questions.stem: Describe the landmarks and structures encountered during aspiration of a knee effusion.
markingGuide: Knee extended and the patella located.
Entry just lateral or medial to the superior pole of the patella.
Needle passes under the patella into the suprapatellar pouch.
Nearby: quadriceps tendon, patella, retinacula, femoral condyle cartilage.
Aseptic technique important to avoid introducing infection.
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar pouch is a continuation of the joint cavity, so fluid pools there. The entry point beside the superior pole allows access without damaging articular cartilage.
